explanations: luna: The verse describes people as dead, then given life, then made to die and live again before returning to God; it sets out the existence-death-return sequence behind the section’s image. | terra: People were lifeless, were given life, will be made to die and given life again, then returned to God; the whole sequence is explicit.
terra: The thunderbolt takes the people while they look on, supplying the death that 2:56 then reverses by raising them.
terra: After the thunderbolt death, the people are raised so that they may give thanks; the ayah explicitly reverses death.
terra: A man has been killed and the killers conceal the act; this supplies the actual corpse whose revival follows in 2:73.

luna: After the murdered man is struck with part of the cow, God brings him to life; the verse explicitly says God thus brings the dead to life, a narrated instance of the section’s death-to-life movement. | terra: A slain person is restored to life as a displayed sign that God gives life to the dead.

luna: The section’s dictionary form for و ج د describes something becoming existent after nonexistence; this verse says God originates the heavens and earth and that when He decrees a thing, it is. It makes that coming-into-being a divine act. | terra: The Originator brings a decreed thing into being by saying “Be”; this is a cosmic formulation of existence after nonexistence, though burial is not in view.
terra: When death comes to Jacob, he addresses his sons about what they will worship after him; this is an actual deathbed farewell spoken by the departing to the living.

luna: The verse says not to call those killed in God’s path dead, for they are alive with their Lord. It reverses the funeral status at the center of the section; 3:169 gives a parallel formulation. | terra: Those killed in God’s path must not be called dead but living, setting a revealed boundary against judging life solely from the corpse and funeral.

luna: The verse describes the waiting period of wives after their husbands die; it gives a concrete life of separation after death, corresponding to the section’s note that farewell extends to the dead.

luna: A people flee death, God tells them to die, then gives them life; this is a collective death-and-return scene, though it does not depict burial. | terra: A multitude fleeing death are made to die and then revived, turning death and renewed life into a collective enacted scene.

luna: The section title uses tabut for a funeral chest; this verse’s التابوت is the covenant chest carrying tranquility and relics, not a corpse. The shared container image marks a specific boundary between the funerary bier and the Ark. | terra: التَّابُوتُ is carried by angels and contains tranquility and family relics; this carried chest bears a sign and inherited remains rather than a dead body.
terra: The king claims “I give life and cause death,” but Abraham’s challenge exposes this as a counterfeit use of the acts the section attributes to God.

luna: A man is made to die for a hundred years and then revived, while the bones of his donkey are reassembled. This gives a concrete case of bodily death and renewed life after decay. | terra: A man is made dead for a hundred years, raised, and shown bones assembled and clothed with flesh; the corpse-to-recreated-body movement is displayed rather than merely asserted.
terra: Abraham is shown how dead birds are restored and summoned, making reassembly and renewed motion perceptible.
terra: God brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living, a compact reciprocal formulation of the boundary crossed by the section.

luna: Jesus says he brings the dead to life by God’s permission; this is a direct scene of death followed by restored life. | terra: Jesus’ sign of giving life to the dead by God’s permission enacts the same passage from corpse to life within worldly time.

luna: The verse forbids calling those killed in God’s way dead, saying they are alive with their Lord; it reverses the funeral status in the section and marks a boundary between bodily death and continued life. | terra: The slain are described as alive and provided for with their Lord, reversing the apparent finality of their deaths.

luna: The verse says every soul tastes death and receives its full reward on the Day of Resurrection; it joins mortality to the life and judgment that follow. | terra: Every soul tastes death and receives full recompense on Resurrection Day, placing death before rather than after the final outcome.

luna: The section notes that an orphan’s status carries the death of a father; this verse protects the property of orphans, giving a concrete consequence of that parental loss, though it does not narrate the death.
luna: The verse orders guardians to test orphans until maturity and then hand over their property; it develops the practical aftermath of the father’s death implicit in orphanhood.
terra: Within the orphan-property passage, people are told to fear leaving weak offspring behind; it makes the parental death presupposed by orphanhood visible.

luna: After killing his brother, one son of Adam sees a crow scratch the earth and learn how to bury the corpse. This is the section’s burial image enacted as a scene. | terra: The crow scratches the earth to show Cain how to conceal his brother’s corpse, staging the section’s act of putting the dead into the ground.
terra: The testament rule explicitly joins travel on the earth with the calamity of death, bringing together the living traveler and the dying person behind the source’s two uses of farewell.

luna: In God’s address to Jesus, raising the dead by God’s permission is recalled among the signs given him; it repeats the section’s passage from death to life in a narrated miracle. | terra: God recalls Jesus bringing the dead out alive by divine permission, repeating the concrete death-to-life sign.

luna: The speakers say that they only die and live in worldly life and will not be raised. This directly rejects the passage from death to a later existence. | terra: The denial “only our worldly life” and “we will not be raised” states the boundary the section’s movement beyond death crosses.
terra: Those who denied raising in 6:29 are made to stand before their Lord and acknowledge its truth, completing objection with encounter.
terra: The unresponsive are set beside “the dead,” whom God will raise and return; the ayah pivots from a figurative deafness to literal resurrection.

luna: God takes people at night, then raises them by day and returns them to life until their appointed term; this links the section’s literal night scene to a reversible passage resembling death. | terra: God takes people during the night and raises them during the day until the fixed term; daily sleep and waking form a reversible counterpart to death and final raising.

luna: When death comes, God’s messengers take the person and he is returned to God, his true Master; it gives the passage from bodily death to return without naming the grave. | terra: Divine messengers take a person at death without neglect, presenting death as a transfer under custody rather than disappearance.
terra: After being taken in death, people are returned to God for judgment, completing the transfer begun in 6:61.
terra: The Creator of heaven and earth says “Be” and it is, while the same ayah names the day of the trumpet; first creation and eschatological reappearance meet in one statement.
terra: In the throes of death the wrongdoers are ordered by the angels to yield their souls, staging the final separation and its unseen witnesses.
terra: People come to God alone “as We created you the first time” and leave their former gifts behind; return is measured against first creation and worldly farewell.
terra: The splitting of seed and kernel is joined to bringing living from dead and dead from living, giving the transition a buried-seed analogue.

luna: The section quotes this verse’s “place of settlement” and “place of deposit” (مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمُسْتَوْدَعٌ) as spanning the passage between being entrusted and remaining; the verse itself locates both in human creation from one soul. | terra: Origin from one soul is followed by مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمُسْتَوْدَعٌ, the stable and entrusted places that the source reads across life, death, and return.

terra: A person described as dead is given life and a light to walk by; physical death-and-revival language is redirected to guidance, just as the source hears funeral language without forcing it onto 93’s surface meaning.
terra: Earth is assigned as a temporary dwelling and provision until a term, establishing the living side of the earth-cycle completed by death and emergence in 7:25.

luna: God says people will live on earth, die there, and be brought out from it; the verse states the soil-to-life passage that the section’s burial and renewed-being image carries. | terra: Life on earth, death in it, and emergence from it are stated as one cycle; the earth is both place of burial and point of renewed appearance.
terra: At death the messengers take the wrongdoers and question them about what they invoked, presenting death as custody followed by interrogation.

luna: Rain revives dead land, and the verse compares this to bringing the dead forth. It gives the same earth-to-life pattern as the section’s burial image. | terra: Rain revives a dead land and the ayah says “thus We bring out the dead,” making earth’s greening a direct analogue for emergence from burial.
terra: Angels take the disbelievers at death while striking them, another concrete form of the soul’s forced departure.
terra: The prohibition on praying over a dead person and standing at his grave stages the funeral rite and graveside directly.
terra: Return to God is grounded in His beginning creation and repeating it, a direct formulation of first and renewed existence.
terra: The opponents acknowledge that God brings living from dead and dead from living, so their own answer supplies a premise for renewed life.
terra: The question asks who begins creation and then repeats it, and the answer names God; repeated creation is used against the deniers’ false objects of worship.

luna: God gives life and causes death, and to Him people return; it states the passage from mortality to return that underlies the image. | terra: God gives life and causes death, and to Him people return; the return prevents death from closing the sequence.
terra: Every creature’s provision is known together with its مُسْتَقَرّ and مُسْتَوْدَع; the same two-place vocabulary as 6:98 extends the image across creaturely lodging and deposit.
terra: When resurrection after death is announced, the disbelievers dismiss it as magic; this is another clearly marked version of the section’s objection scene.

luna: The objection asks whether becoming dust is followed by a new creation. It restates the section’s precise passage from burial to renewed existence. | terra: The objection puts becoming dust beside being in a new creation, directly matching the section’s burial and re-existence pairing.
terra: Death comes at the condemned person from every side yet he does not die, a punitive refusal of the release ordinarily marked by death.
luna: The verse says that if God wills He can remove people and bring a new creation; it extends the section’s new-being theme from an individual burial to replacement of a whole people.
luna: This verse says such replacement is not difficult for God, completing the new-creation claim in 14:19.
terra: God gives life, causes death, and remains the inheritor, placing creaturely mortality inside continuing divine possession.
terra: The invoked beings are “dead, not living” and do not know when they will be raised, applying death-and-resurrection language to powerless objects of worship.
terra: Angels take the souls of wrongdoers, who then offer submission; it forms the adverse counterpart to the peaceful taking in 16:32.
terra: Angels take the good at death with a greeting of peace and entry into the Garden, turning the final farewell into a welcome elsewhere.

luna: The deniers swear that God will not raise the dead; 16:39 answers that He will raise them to make clear what they disputed. This row states the denial answered by the section’s resurrection arc. | terra: The emphatic oath that God will not raise whoever dies is answered as a binding promise, making the denial and answer explicit in one ayah.

luna: The section’s dictionary form for و ج د names existence after nonexistence; here God says that when He wills a thing, He commands it and it is, a specific formulation of coming into being. | terra: Following the denied promise to raise the dead, God’s word to a willed thing is simply that it be, and it is; existence after nonexistence answers the denial.
terra: The ashamed father considers hiding his living daughter in the dust, turning burial from care for a corpse into an act against life.
terra: Water gives life to earth after its death; although resurrection is not stated in this ayah, the visible earthward transition concretely parallels the image.
luna: The verse contrasts what passes away with what remains with God; it makes mortality and lasting existence perceptible in the section’s move from burial to renewed life.

luna: The deniers ask whether bones and fragments can be raised as a new creation. It is the same objection to renewed being after bodily decomposition that the section cites in 32:10. | terra: Bones and crumbled remains are set against خَلْقًا جَدِيدًا, another direct formulation of the section’s corpse-to-new-creation transition.
terra: The answer tells deniers to imagine themselves stone or iron, showing that even a form they think resistant to decay cannot block the Creator’s return.

luna: After the question about bones in 17:49, this verse asks who will bring the deniers back and answers: the One who created them the first time. It supplies the first-creation argument for return. | terra: The answer identifies the restorer as the One who originated them أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ, making first creation the warrant for return.
terra: God’s call receives their response and brings them out of their former condition, completing the answer begun in 17:51.
luna: The deniers ask if bones and dust will be raised as a new creation; this repeats the section’s central dispute with the corpse reduced to earth.
terra: The Creator of the heavens and earth is said able to create people’s like and to have set a term for them, a later reprise of the answer to 17:49’s denial.
terra: The companions’ hearing is sealed in the cave for years, beginning the enclosed, deathlike sleep from which 18:12 raises them.
terra: God raises the sleepers after their long enclosed sleep, beginning the episode that 18:21 explicitly makes evidence for resurrection.
terra: The sleepers look awake although asleep and their bodies are turned, holding visible signs of life and deathlike repose together during their long enclosure.
terra: “Thus We raised them” brings the sleepers back into speech and movement after their deathlike interval, a lived analogue of renewed existence.
terra: The sleepers are disclosed so people may know the resurrection promise is true, and the debate about building over them gives their resting place the aspect of a tomb.
terra: Those presented before God are told that they have come as they were created the first time, making resurrection a return to first origination.
terra: At judgment people find وَجَدُوا what they did made present, حَاضِرًا; the source root of “finding/existence” thus meets post-death disclosure rather than creation itself.

luna: The section notes that the orphan named in 93:6 stands behind a dead father; here two orphan boys’ righteous father is explicitly recalled, and their hidden treasure is kept for them until maturity. The father’s death is presupposed by their orphan status rather than narrated. | terra: Two orphan boys are named together with their righteous father and the inheritance hidden for them; the context makes the absent father behind يَتِيم visible.
terra: God reminds Zechariah, “I created you before when you were nothing,” stating the source’s definition of existence after nonexistence almost exactly.
terra: Peace attends John on the day of birth, the day of death, and the day he is raised alive, placing a whole human course in the section’s order.
terra: Jesus names his birth, death, and being raised alive as three marked days, repeating the same life-to-death-to-life sequence in first-person speech.

luna: The human asks whether he will be brought out alive after he has died; this is a direct question about life after death, continuing the creation-from-nothing discussion in 19:67. | terra: The human being asks whether, after dying, he will be brought out alive; the wording directly crosses death, emergence, and life.

luna: The section’s dictionary form for the root و ج د describes a thing coming into existence after nonexistence; this verse asks whether the human remembers being created when previously nothing. | terra: The reply recalls that God created the human being before when he was nothing, exactly matching the source’s “being after non-being” sense.
terra: Moses is put alive as an infant into التَّابُوتِ and cast on the water; the coffin-shaped chest carries vulnerable life toward rescue rather than a corpse toward burial.
terra: The living child from the chest is returned to his mother so that she may cease grieving, completing the reversal of funeral farewell begun in 20:39.

luna: The section identifies 93:4’s al-ākhirah word with second creation; in God’s answer within Moses’ account, people are made from earth, returned to it, then brought out another time (أُخْرَىٰ). This completes the transition disputed in 32:10. | terra: God’s answer names the whole movement: creation from earth, return into it, and another bringing-out, تَارَةً أُخْرَىٰ; this is the section’s funeral-to-second-creation arc in one ayah.
terra: The one entering Hell neither dies there nor lives, a suspended boundary that reverses the section’s directional passage from death into renewed life.

luna: The section identifies the root of 93:11’s “tell” with the dictionary form الحدوث, coming into being after not-being; this verse uses a related form for a newly arriving reminder. Its context is new revelation, not bodily resurrection, so the link is lexical and limited.
terra: Every soul tastes death and is then returned to God, stating the universal departure and return that frame the image.

luna: The verse says God will repeat creation as He began it, comparing the Day to a scroll rolled up; it directly states second creation and adds the image of a written record. | terra: As creation began أَوَّلَ خَلْقٍ, God will repeat it; the image of rolling the sky also places first origination and re-creation in one promise.

luna: The verse moves from human creation from dust to the revival of dead earth, then uses that sign in its address about resurrection. It connects earth as origin, burial-place, and renewed life. | terra: The ayah runs from earthen origin through womb stages and death, then revives dead earth as evidence for renewed human life; it develops both halves of the section’s passage.

luna: Following the earth and human-creation signs in 22:5, this verse states that God is true and gives life to the dead; it makes the resurrection claim explicit. | terra: Following the creation and dead-earth demonstration, the ayah states that God gives life to the dead, identifying the transition displayed in 22:5.

luna: The verse joins the coming Hour to God’s raising those in the graves, making the funeral ground the place from which the next life begins. | terra: The coming Hour culminates in God raising those in the graves, turning burial into renewed presence.
terra: God gives life, causes death, and then gives life again, a compact statement of the section’s direction.
terra: Human creation begins from an extract of clay, opening a sequence that proceeds through womb, death, and resurrection in 23:13–16.
terra: The drop is placed in قَرَارٍ مَكِينٍ, a secure lodging; this supplies a life-side counterpart to the section’s grave and depository language.
terra: After successive formations God produces خَلْقًا آخَرَ, an “other creation”; within 23:12–16 it anticipates the later passage from death to raising.

luna: After describing human formation earlier, this verse says people will surely die; 23:16 gives the separate contribution of being raised on the Day of Resurrection. | terra: ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ لَمَيِّتُونَ places death after the first formation and before the next ayah’s resurrection.

luna: The verse says people will be raised on the Day of Resurrection after the death stated in 23:15, completing the life-to-death-to-life sequence. | terra: ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ تُبْعَثُونَ completes 23:12–15’s ordered movement from earth and gestation through death to renewed life.

luna: The people ask whether, after dying and becoming dust and bones, they will be brought out; the verse directly disputes the same post-burial emergence. | terra: A messenger’s opponents ridicule the promise that after death, dust, and bones they will be brought out.
terra: “Far, far is what you are promised” records the opponents’ scornful stance toward the promised emergence described in 23:35.
terra: Their counterclaim restricts existence to worldly dying and living and denies being raised, clarifying the resistance voiced in 23:35.
terra: God gives life and causes death; the accompanying alternation of night and day adds a recurring visible cycle to the claim.

luna: The speakers ask whether people will be raised after death, dust, and bones. This is another direct version of the section’s burial-to-new-creation question. | terra: Death, dust, bones, and being raised are again placed in one skeptical question, a close parallel to the objection quoted in the section.
terra: The deniers say that they and their fathers were promised this before, adding generational memory to their dust-and-bones objection in 23:82.

luna: At death, a person asks to be sent back so he can act rightly; this gives the funeral transition a human voice at the moment life ends. | terra: At death a person asks to be sent back, staging the moment when farewell becomes irreversible.

luna: The answer to the request in 23:99 places a barrier behind the dead until the day they are raised. It marks the boundary between burial and the later return the section evokes. | terra: A barrier stands behind the dead until the day they are raised, locating burial-time between departure and renewed existence.

terra: The thirsty person “finds” the mirage to be nothing and then finds God there for reckoning; the source’s و ج د family here turns on absent versus encountered reality in an afterlife-facing image.
terra: False gods are themselves created and possess neither death, life, nor resurrection; their incapacity sets a boundary around acts that belong to the Creator.
terra: God makes night a covering, sleep a repose, and day a rising; the ayah joins the source’s night-cover image to a daily analogue of death and resurrection.
terra: Abraham names God as the One who causes him to die and then gives him life, a personal confession of the section’s movement.

luna: The verse asks who begins creation and then repeats it; the repeated making is the exact idea the section hears in its al-ākhirah word. | terra: Beginning creation and repeating it are posed as a challenge about divine identity, making renewed origination the decisive act.
terra: The disbelievers ask whether they and their fathers will be brought out after becoming dust, making emergence from ancestral burial explicit.
terra: The complaint that they and their fathers had long been promised resurrection continues 27:67’s image of ancestral dust.
luna: The verse says the dead cannot be made to hear; it gives the same explicit limit on speech across graves that bounds the section’s lexical movement toward narration.
luna: The verse asks whether people have seen God begin creation and then repeat it; this is the section’s second-creation claim stated as a direct question.

luna: The next verse directs people to observe how creation began and says God will bring about the latter creation; it completes the first-making/re-creation claim in 29:19. | terra: The command to observe how creation began culminates in النَّشْأَةَ الْآخِرَةَ, directly naming the “later/second creation” sense highlighted in the source.

luna: The verse says every soul tastes death and then returns to God, a direct formulation of the death-to-return movement in the section. | terra: Every soul tastes death and is then returned to God, repeating the same death-to-return order in the context of migration and worship.

luna: God originates creation and repeats it, then people are returned to Him; this directly matches the section’s second existence. | terra: God begins creation, repeats it, and then people are returned to Him, stating the full direction in one ayah.

luna: The verse turns living into dead and dead into living, revives earth after its death, and says people will be brought out; it gathers the section’s two movements in one formulation. | terra: Bringing living from dead and dead from living is joined to reviving earth and “thus you are brought out,” a precise transition across the boundary.
luna: When God calls people from the earth, they come forth; this is a concise scene of emergence from the ground that completes the section’s burial-to-life movement.

luna: The verse says God originates creation and repeats it, and that repeating it is easy for Him; it gives the section’s renewed-creation claim in another direct formulation. | terra: The One who begins creation repeats it; the repeated formula directly supports the source’s reading of a later creation after the first.
luna: God creates, provides, causes death, and gives life again; this explicit sequence matches the section’s movement from existence through death to life.

luna: The verse points to dead earth revived by rain and says God is capable of all things; it gives another specific earth-after-death analogy for the section’s renewed-life theme. | terra: The effects of mercy revive earth after death, then the same Giver is named as the One who revives the dead.
luna: The verse says the dead cannot hear a call; it marks the limit of communication across burial, a counterpoint to the section’s movement from death-associated words toward telling.
terra: The creation and resurrection of all people are said to be like those of a single soul, explicitly joining the two creative acts.

luna: The section gives burial as a dictionary sense of 93:7’s ض ل ل root; here the speakers ask whether, after being lost into earth, they will be in a new creation. It is the Quranic objection that makes burial the question of renewed existence. | terra: The deniers use ضَلَلْنَا فِي الْأَرْضِ for bodies lost into earth and immediately reject a “new creation,” directly joining the section’s burial sense of the ض ل ل family to re-creation.

luna: The verse after 32:10 says the appointed Angel of Death takes people and they are returned to their Lord. It contributes the death-and-return sequence that the preceding question about becoming a new creation leaves unresolved. | terra: The angel of death takes people and they are then returned to their Lord, spelling out the meeting whose denial closes 32:10.
terra: When the meeting denied in 32:10 occurs, the guilty stand before their Lord and ask to be returned, showing the promised emergence and its irreversible direction.

luna: The deniers ask whether, after being torn apart, they will be in a new creation. The verse directly contests the same possibility of life after bodily dissolution. | terra: The mock announcement links complete bodily disintegration to خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ, the same apparent gap between corpse and renewed existence.
luna: After the new-creation question in 34:7, this verse locates the accusers in disbelief in the Hereafter and error; it identifies the stance behind their resistance to renewed existence.

luna: After describing dead land made alive by rain, the verse says resurrection is likewise; it supplies an earth-based analogy for life after death. | terra: Rain revives dead land and the ayah explicitly identifies that scene with النُّشُورُ, resurrection.

luna: The verse says the living and dead are not alike and that a messenger cannot make those in graves hear. It marks a boundary between the section’s death vocabulary and its later language of being and telling. | terra: The living and dead are not equal, and those in graves cannot be made to hear; the grave here marks the boundary of prophetic address rather than the later raising.
terra: The condemned are neither finished by death nor relieved, extending life without the death-and-return transition developed in the section.
luna: The verse says God gives life to the dead and records what people send ahead and their traces; it joins resurrection to what remains of a person’s actions.
terra: Dead earth is revived and grain is brought out from it, offering emergence of life from buried ground as a sign alongside the later bone-resurrection argument.

luna: At the trumpet, people come out of their graves and hasten to their Lord. The grave opening is the scene that carries the section’s move from burial to renewed existence. | terra: At the trumpet blast people hasten from the graves, a direct scene of the buried becoming present again.

luna: Those raised in 36:51 ask who woke them from their resting place; the verse answers that this is what the Merciful promised. Its contribution is the dead person’s own recognition of resurrection. | terra: Those newly raised ask who awakened them from their resting place; their speech preserves the grave-as-resting-place image while recognizing resurrection.
terra: After emergence from the graves, one cry leaves everyone brought present before God, completing 36:51–52’s scene.

luna: The challenger asks who can give life to bones after they have crumbled; this makes the decomposed body itself the test of renewed existence. | terra: A man displays decayed bones and asks who can revive them, turning the denial into a visible corpse-remains scene.

luna: The answer to the broken-bone challenge in 36:78 is that the One who made them the first time will revive them. It links the first making to the life that follows bodily decay. | terra: The answer names the One who produced the bones أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ; first origination guarantees their revival.

luna: After the answer about reviving bones in 36:79, this verse asks whether the Creator of the heavens and earth can create their like; it adds the scale-of-creation argument for re-creation. | terra: The Creator of the heavens and earth is able to create people’s like, continuing the answer to the decayed-bones objection.

luna: The section’s dictionary form for و ج د describes what comes to exist after not existing; this verse says that when God wills a thing, it is by His command, giving another explicit formulation of origination. | terra: A thing exists when God wills it and says “Be”; after the bone-resurrection argument, this states the source’s coming-into-being sense as the mechanism of the answer.

luna: The deniers ask whether people will be raised after death, dust, and bones; the bodily stages match the section’s movement from burial toward another existence. | terra: The deniers ask whether death, dust, and bones can end in being raised, directly staging the section’s burial-to-creation question.
terra: They add their “first forefathers,” extending the question from one corpse to generations already buried.
terra: The answer “yes” reverses the denial of 37:16–17 and says they will return humbled.

luna: A companion is asked whether, after death and becoming dust and bones, he will be judged; the question again places bodily decay against life after death. | terra: A remembered skeptic had asked whether death, dust, and bones could end in judgment; the question is recalled from within the afterlife that answers it.

luna: God takes souls at death and during sleep, retaining those for whom death is decreed and releasing the others. It links night’s withdrawal to death while preserving the boundary between sleep and final death. | terra: God takes souls at death and in sleep, retaining the one sentenced to death and releasing the other; it distinguishes temporary covering/rest from final departure.
terra: The trumpet causes all in the heavens and earth to die, then a second blast leaves them standing and looking; death and renewed embodied presence are shown in immediate succession.

luna: The speakers acknowledge two deaths and two lives before confessing their sins; this is a compact formulation of death followed by renewed existence. | terra: At judgment people confess two deaths and two lives, explicitly recognizing repeated passage across the life-death boundary they had denied.
terra: Creation from dust and a drop proceeds through life stages to death, tracing existence from nonbeing toward the funeral threshold.

luna: The verse joins giving life and death to God’s command that a thing exist when He decrees it; it connects the image’s death-to-life passage with creation by divine command. | terra: The One who gives life and death brings a thing into being by saying “Be”; this joins death-to-life with the source’s “made existent after not existing” gloss.

luna: God revives the earth after its death, and the verse asks whether the One who did so can give life to the dead. It explicitly bridges the dead ground to the dead person. | terra: The lifeless earth stirs and grows with water, and its reviver is declared able to give life to the dead.

luna: God sends water and revives a dead land, then says people will likewise be brought out. The verse makes the earth’s return to life an explicit counterpart to resurrection. | terra: Measured water revives a dead land and “thus you will be brought out,” connecting emergence from earth to resurrection.
terra: God gives life and causes death and is Lord of the hearers and their first fathers, joining mortality to the generations invoked by deniers.
terra: The deniers call death only مَوْتَتُنَا الْأُولَىٰ and deny being raised, bringing the “first” root into the death-versus-second-life dispute.
terra: The deniers demand that their fathers be brought back, making ancestral death the test they set against resurrection.

luna: The deniers say there is only worldly life, with people dying and living while time destroys them; this is the contrary boundary to the section’s movement into life after death. | terra: The claim that people merely die and live and that time destroys them voices the denial of any passage beyond worldly succession.
terra: The opponents’ sole argument is the challenge to bring their fathers, turning the buried previous generation into their demanded proof.

luna: God gives life and death and gathers people for the Day, while the verse records that many do not know this; it makes the section’s life-beyond-death boundary explicit. | terra: God’s answer orders life, death, and gathering on the Resurrection Day, correcting 45:24’s attempt to close the sequence at death.
terra: A child rejects his parents’ promise that he will be brought out after generations have passed, combining family farewell, ancestral death, and resurrection denial.

luna: The verse argues that the Creator of the heavens and earth can give life to the dead; it directly supports the section’s transition from death to renewed existence. | terra: Creation of the heavens and earth is invoked as proof that God can give life to the dead, answering resurrection denial with prior creation.
terra: Angels take the disbelievers while striking faces and backs, continuing the Qur’anic scenes of death as an enacted transfer.

luna: The disbelievers ask whether, after dying and becoming dust, they will return; this repeats the section’s burial-to-new-creation question, alongside the burial sense of 93:7’s ض ل ل root. | terra: The objection “when we have died and become dust” calls bodily return remote, voicing the same denial that the section answers through burial and new creation.

luna: The answer to the dust objection in 50:3 says God knows what the earth diminishes from bodies and has a preserving record. It adds that bodily loss into earth does not erase the person from divine knowledge. | terra: God knows what the earth diminishes of the dead and has a preserving record, directly answering 50:3’s fear that burial makes the body irretrievably lost.

luna: The verse describes God bringing grain from dead land and providing for His servants; in the same surah that says the earth diminishes bodies, it gives an earth-revival counterpart to resurrection.

luna: The verse asks whether the first creation exhausted God, then says the deniers remain confused about a new creation; it directly contests the same second-creation question as 32:10. | terra: Failure is denied in الْخَلْقِ الْأَوَّلِ, while the deniers remain confused about خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ; first and renewed creation are explicitly paired.
terra: The stupor of death arrives with truth, presenting the actual threshold that the section’s farewell vocabulary surrounds.
terra: The trumpet follows the death-threshold in 50:19 and announces the threatened day, moving immediately from dying to resurrection.
terra: “We give life and cause death, and to Us is the destination” joins mortality to an onward return in the resurrection passage.
terra: The earth splits away from people as they emerge rapidly; burial ground itself opens into resurrection.

luna: The section’s dictionary form for و ج د describes existence after nonexistence; this verse asks whether people were created from nothing or created themselves, making the origin question explicit. | terra: The question whether people were created from nothing or are creators presses the source’s concern with how what was not comes to be, though it does not itself stage burial.
luna: The verse places the final and the first with God; it echoes the al-ākhirah/al-ūlā pair named in the section and the passage from first life to what follows.

luna: The verse says God causes death and life; it gives the section’s death-to-life movement in a compressed form without its burial scene. | terra: God causes death and gives life, immediately before the passage’s statement of the other creation.
terra: A drop when emitted supplies the first-creation detail between God’s giving life and death in 53:44 and the other creation in 53:47.

luna: The section reads 93:4’s al-ākhirah-root word through second creation; this verse explicitly names the other creation (النَّشْأَةَ الْأُخْرَىٰ), directly matching renewed existence. | terra: وَأَنَّ عَلَيْهِ النَّشْأَةَ الْأُخْرَىٰ states that the other creation belongs to God, an exact Qur’anic realization of the section’s gloss of the ء خ ر family.

luna: The verse depicts people coming out of graves with humbled eyes, dispersed like locusts. The grave-opening scene directly parallels the section’s passage from burial to life again. | terra: People come out of the graves like scattered locusts, giving the section’s movement out of burial a vivid collective scene.

luna: The deniers ask whether they will be raised after dying and becoming dust and bones, directly repeating the image’s central objection. | terra: The objection joins death, dust, bones, and resurrection in the same order as the section’s passage from burial language to renewed existence.
terra: Mention of the first forefathers makes long-buried generations part of 56:47’s objection.
terra: The reply gathers الْأَوَّلِينَ وَالْآخِرِينَ, using the first/later polarity central to the section’s reading of creation.
terra: All those generations are gathered at an appointed time, answering the dispersed dust and bones of 56:47.
terra: “We created you” confronts disbelief just before the passage moves through procreation, death, replacement, and first creation.
terra: Emitted seed is presented as the material beginning of a life that the passage later carries through death and another formation.
terra: The question whether humans create that seed or God does makes divine origination the premise for the following death-and-replacement sequence.

luna: God decrees death among people and says no one can escape or be prevented; it makes the funeral image’s mortality a divine limit. | terra: God’s ordaining of death opens a sequence about replacement and a form of creation not yet known.

luna: The verse says God can replace people and create them in a form they do not know; it completes the death decree in 56:60 with renewed creation. | terra: God can replace people and produce them in a form they do not know, supplying the renewed-existence side of 56:60’s death.

luna: The verse recalls the first creation and asks why people do not remember; it supplies first-making as evidence for the second creation in the preceding two ayat. | terra: Knowledge of النَّشْأَةَ الْأُولَىٰ is invoked as evidence for the post-death transformation in 56:60–61, pairing first creation with another.

luna: The passage begins its death scene when the soul reaches the throat; it supplies the moment of departure that precedes the section’s shroud, farewell, and burial image. | terra: The soul reaching the throat presents the same deathbed boundary as 75:26 in the presence of those saying farewell.

luna: The verse says the onlookers are watching as the soul reaches the throat in 56:83; it adds the witnesses present at death before the ensuing challenge about return. | terra: Those around the dying person look on, making 56:83’s soul-at-the-throat moment a witnessed farewell.

luna: The verse says God is nearer to the dying person than the watching people, though they do not see; it locates divine presence in the death scene begun in 56:83. | terra: God is nearer to the dying person than the witnesses can see, adding unseen divine presence to the human farewell scene.
luna: After the soul reaches the throat in 56:83, the verse challenges the onlookers to return it if they are not answerable to God; it makes the limit between death and human power explicit.

luna: The next verse completes the challenge in 56:86: if the onlookers are truthful, they should return the soul. Its contribution is the final impossibility in this death scene. | terra: The witnesses are challenged to return the departing soul if they are beyond judgment; their inability marks death’s one-way boundary before resurrection.
terra: The One who owns the heavens and earth gives life and causes death, identifying both thresholds as divine acts.
terra: The declaration that God revives earth after its death supplies a concise natural analogue for life after burial.
terra: The death from which people flee will meet them, after which they are returned to the Knower; attempted avoidance ends in departure and return.

luna: The deniers say they will not be raised, and the reply swears that they will be. This is an explicit boundary between denial of resurrection and the section’s renewed-being image. | terra: Those who claim they will never be raised receive a direct divine oath that they will be raised and told what they did.
terra: لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يُحْدِثُ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ أَمْرًا uses the source’s ح د ث family for God bringing about a new state after the former one, a non-funerary but relevant sense of coming-to-be.

luna: God creates death and life to test people; the verse presents death as part of a purposeful passage rather than an end, matching the section’s movement beyond burial. | terra: Death and life are themselves created in an ordered test, so death is a made stage rather than the end of existence.

luna: People emerge from the graves hurriedly on the day they are summoned; this is a direct Quranic scene of burial ending in rising. | terra: They emerge rapidly from graves as if racing toward a marker, an explicit reversal of emplacement in the grave.

luna: The verse says God caused people to grow from the earth like plants; it connects human existence to the same earth from which the section says the buried are brought back. | terra: Human creation is pictured as growth from the earth, beginning the same earthward and earth-outward movement that the section develops.

luna: The verse says God returns people to the earth and then brings them out from it; it gives the clearest parallel to burial followed by emergence. | terra: ثُمَّ يُعِيدُكُمْ فِيهَا وَيُخْرِجُكُمْ إِخْرَاجًا explicitly returns people to earth and brings them out, completing 71:17’s creation image as burial and resurrection.

luna: The source section’s dictionary gloss for 93:2 connects covering to a dead body; this verse addresses a living person wrapped in garments at night. The parallel is the covered figure, with the difference in life status explicit.
luna: The command to stand at night follows the wrapped figure in 73:1; it completes that living, nocturnal scene and contrasts with the burial covering in the section’s dictionary gloss.

luna: The source section’s dictionary gloss for 93:2 describes cloth covering a corpse; here the addressee is “the wrapped one” (الْمُدَّثِّرُ), a living person, so the shared covering becomes a clear reversal of the shroud scene.

luna: After addressing the living “wrapped one” in 74:1, this verse commands him to rise and warn; it adds movement and proclamation after covering, in contrast to the corpse in the section’s dictionary gloss.

luna: The verse asks whether the human thinks God will not gather his bones; it makes bodily reassembly the concrete question after death. | terra: The human being doubts that God will gather his bones, reducing the resurrection objection to the dispersed remains of a corpse.

luna: The answer in the next verse says God can restore even the fingertips; it adds precise reconstruction to the gathering of bones in 75:3. | terra: God answers that even the fingertips can be proportioned again, making renewed embodiment more exact than merely collecting bones.
terra: On the resurrection day the settled destination is to the Lord, giving the “resting place” vocabulary an eschatological endpoint rather than a grave.

luna: The verse depicts the soul reaching the collarbones, the threshold of death; it gives the section’s farewell and burial image the preceding moment of bodily departure. | terra: Life reaching the collarbones stages the physical onset of death and the beginning of final farewell.

luna: As death arrives in 75:26, people ask who can cure or save the dying person; this verse adds the futile appeal at the point of departure. | terra: At the deathbed people ask who might heal or save the dying person, continuing the farewell scene between the collarbones and recognized parting.

luna: The next verse says the dying person knows it is the moment of separation; it makes farewell explicit within the death scene begun in 75:26. | terra: The dying person realizes أَنَّهُ الْفِرَاقُ, “that it is the parting,” making the section’s farewell-to-the-dead sense explicit.

luna: The verse describes the legs being joined as death advances, continuing the bodily scene of departure before the return to God in 75:30. | terra: One leg is wound with the other as death closes over the body, supplying the bodily middle of 75:26–30’s departure scene.

luna: The verse says that day the person is driven to his Lord; it completes the death sequence in 75:26–29 with the movement to divine return. | terra: The dying person’s course is then toward the Lord, carrying the deathbed parting into the encounter denied in 32:10.
terra: The human being was a drop of emitted fluid, beginning the first-creation proof that culminates in reviving the dead.
terra: The drop becomes a clinging form which God creates and proportions, displaying formation from an earlier unformed state.
terra: Formation as male and female completes the first bodily creation recalled before 75:40 draws the inference to reviving the dead.

luna: After describing human creation and development, the verse asks whether God cannot give life to the dead; it states the section’s renewed-life claim as the conclusion of a creation argument. | terra: The completed first-creation account ends by asking whether its Creator can give life to the dead, making the inference explicit.

luna: The section’s dictionary form for و ج د names coming to exist after not existing; this verse asks whether a time passed when the human was not even a thing mentioned. | terra: Humanity once was not a thing mentioned, supplying the “before it existed” half of the source’s explanation of coming into being.

luna: After asking whether a time passed when the human was nothing in 76:1, this verse says God created the human from a mixed drop and tested him; it completes the passage from nonexistence to embodied life.
terra: Creation from a lowly fluid begins a passage that moves through a secure lodging and then the earth’s containment of living and dead.
terra: The fluid is placed in قَرَارٍ مَكِينٍ, a secure repository that forms a life-side counterpart to the earth as container in 77:25–26.
terra: The womb-deposit remains until a known measure, distinguishing its timed custody from the later custody of the dead in earth.
terra: The earth is called كِفَاتًا, a containing place; the next ayah specifies that it gathers both living and dead, closely matching the section’s lodging and burial places.
terra: أَحْيَاءً وَأَمْوَاتًا makes the earth of 77:25 a receptacle for living and dead together, a compact boundary between dwelling and grave.

luna: The deniers ask whether they will be returned to their former state; 79:11 specifies the decayed bones they mean. This row contributes their question about return after death. | terra: The deniers ask whether they will be returned to the former state, posing renewal as a reversal back into life.

luna: The next part of the question in 79:10 asks whether they will return when they have become decayed bones; it makes bodily dissolution the obstacle to renewed life. | terra: Their question about decayed bones gives the bodily and funerary substance of the “return” in 79:10.

luna: They call the return in 79:10–11 a ruinous return. This verse gives the resistance to the same resurrection the section traces from burial to new existence. | terra: The deniers call the proposed return a losing one, preserving their dismissive stance between the decayed-bones question and the trumpet’s answer.

luna: The answer says there will be only one blast; 79:14 gives its immediate result. It supplies the decisive act that ends the deniers’ imagined impossibility of return. | terra: A single blast is the act that reverses the condition of the decayed bones in 79:11.

luna: After the single blast in 79:13, people are suddenly awake on the earth’s surface. It completes the passage from the bones imagined below ground to life above it. | terra: After that blast they are suddenly upon the earth’s surface, completing movement from buried remains to visible presence.

luna: The section moves from a corpse covered and buried toward new existence; this verse states that God causes a human to die and gives him burial, naming the funeral act directly. | terra: ثُمَّ أَمَاتَهُ فَأَقْبَرَهُ places death and burial in immediate sequence, making literal the funeral background heard in the source roots.

luna: After death and burial in 80:21, this verse says that when God wills, He raises the person (أَنشَرَهُ). It supplies the image’s movement from burial to renewed life. | terra: After 80:21’s burial, ثُمَّ إِذَا شَاءَ أَنْشَرَهُ moves from the grave to being raised, completing exactly the section’s directional sequence.
terra: The buried-alive girl is made present and questioned; unlike ordinary burial after death, this grave was used to kill a living child.
terra: The question “for what sin was she killed?” exposes the living burial of 81:8 as murder, sharply reversing the proper order of death and interment.

luna: The verse says graves will be overturned; it directly stages the opening of burial places at the transition to judgment. | terra: وَإِذَا الْقُبُورُ بُعْثِرَتْ makes the graves themselves overturned and emptied, exposing what burial had covered.
terra: The defrauders are asked whether they think they will be raised, directing moral forgetfulness to renewed existence.
terra: Their raising is assigned to a tremendous day, specifying the time implied by 83:4.
terra: On that day humanity stands before the Lord of the worlds, supplying the bodily presence and meeting produced by the raising.
terra: The earth casts out what is within it and becomes empty; in the judgment sequence this pictures the buried released from their repository.

luna: The verse states that God originates and repeats creation, directly echoing the section’s passage from not-being to being again. | terra: إِنَّهُ هُوَ يُبْدِئُ وَيُعِيدُ compresses first origination and return into paired divine acts.
terra: The command that the human consider what he was created from opens a first-origination proof of his return.
terra: Creation from an emitted fluid supplies the material starting point of the return argument.
terra: The fluid’s emergence from within the body completes the first-formation detail on which the following claim of return rests.
terra: God is declared able to return the human being, turning the remembered first origin of 86:5–7 toward renewed existence.
terra: In the great Fire a person neither dies nor lives, repeating the exceptional state in which the normal death-life sequence is withheld.
luna: The verse says people choose the nearer life; it supplies the contrast to the section’s 93:4 movement from the first life toward the hereafter.

luna: The verse says the hereafter is better and more lasting; it makes explicit the lasting side of the passage from this life toward what follows. | terra: وَالْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ closely echoes 93:4 while making the “later” realm enduring, grounding the source’s move from first life toward what follows it.
terra: The tranquil soul is addressed directly, opening a farewell that becomes a summons to return.
terra: The soul is told to return to its Lord, satisfied and accepted, turning departure from the former life into arrival.
terra: Entry among God’s servants gives the returning soul a new company after its individual farewell.
terra: Entry into Paradise completes the sequence as welcome into another abode.

luna: The source section’s dictionary gloss for 93:2’s sajā includes a burial covering; this verse pictures night covering the day/sun. The connection is only the covering scene, not a claim that the verse depicts death.
luna: The source section’s dictionary gloss for 93:2’s sajā includes a cloth spread over the dead; here night itself covers, so the covering scene echoes that gloss, while this ayah speaks of night.

luna: The verse says the first and the hereafter belong to God; its surah also opens with night covering and day appearing, so it brings together the section’s night-covering and first/afterlife word-pair.
luna: The earth is shaken with its final shaking; 99:2 supplies the next verse’s detail that it casts out its burdens. This row contributes the upheaval that opens the burial scene.

luna: The earth casts out its burdens after the shaking in 99:1, a direct image of what was held within the ground coming out. | terra: The earth casts out its burdens; in the resurrection sequence, what had been deposited in it is brought forth.
terra: The resurrecting earth then تُحَدِّثُ أَخْبَارَهَا, joining the source section’s ح د ث “tell/come to be” root to a scene where the buried have just emerged.

luna: The verse asks whether people know that what is in the graves will be scattered out. It names the buried contents that the section’s burial image leaves under the earth. | terra: The ayah asks about the moment when what is in the graves is scattered out, directly moving hidden corpses into disclosure.
